claims.text: PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles can be prepared through a colloid-based route.
PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles can catalyze nitrobenzene hydrogenation to aniline.
Rapid-quench processing enhances atomistic mixing in noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid-quench processing enhances mixing by accelerating atomic diffusion.
Rapid quenching suppresses elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation.
Suppression of elemental segregation produces a more homogeneous nanoparticle structure.
Rapid-quenched nanoparticles will have a narrower particle-size distribution than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
A narrow particle-size distribution is evidence of uniform elemental distribution.
Rapid quenching preserves a high-temperature homogeneous alloy state by freezing in the mixed atomic configuration.
Greater structural uniformity leads to isolated noble-metal active sites.
Alloying Co, Cu, and Ni with Pt and Pd can produce isolated Pt and Pd sites in PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
Isolated noble-metal sites increase nitrobenzene hydrogenation activity.
Rapid-quenched nanoparticles will have a higher turnover frequency than otherwise identical slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Slow-cooled nanoparticles are expected to exhibit greater elemental segregation.
Slow-cooled nanoparticles are expected to exhibit greater variability in catalytic performance.
The cooling-rate effect should disappear at low temperatures because atomic diffusion is negligible.
The cooling-rate effect should disappear at ultra-high temperatures because atomic diffusion becomes complete regardless of cooling rate.

contradictions.description: Rapid-quench cooling is said to accelerate or enhance atomic diffusion, while the proposed freezing mechanism depends on quenching rapidly arresting diffusion before segregation occurs. The hypothesis does not distinguish high-temperature diffusion before quenching from diffusion during the quench.
